title: Protecting Focus in a Busy Team
summary: Focus breaks down at the team level, so solo hacks only go so far. What research on interruptions shows, and the norms that give engineers real thinking time back.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Nobody on the team is slacking. Replies come in under a minute. People hop on calls, review PRs, keep an eye on the incident channel and unblock each other all day. And yet the one design doc that needs two hours of real thinking has been "almost done" for three weeks.

That's what attention trouble looks like in a team that seems healthy. Every interruption is reasonable on its own: a quick question, a five-minute call, a review request with no context, a meeting that could have been a written decision. Added up, they leave nobody a stretch long enough to do the hard part.

Solo focus hacks only go so far

Most focus advice is personal: close the tabs, mute the phone, try a timer. Those habits help. They stop working when the whole team rewards instant replies and constant availability, because whoever goes dark for two hours looks like the one dropping the ball.

Leslie Perlow watched this happen during a nine-month field study of a software team building a color laser printer (Perlow, "The Time Famine," Administrative Science Quarterly, 1999). Engineers were interrupted constantly. A crisis mindset kept the interruptions coming, and the reward system favored individual heroics, the people who swooped in to fix things. Everyone felt they had too much to do and too little time to do it. Perlow called it a time famine and traced it to how the group used time together.

What an interruption actually costs

In a lab study by Gloria Mark and colleagues, people interrupted while working through email finished their tasks faster than people left alone, with no difference in quality. Sounds like good news until you read the rest: the interrupted group reported more stress, higher frustration, more time pressure and more effort (Mark, Gudith and Klocke, CHI 2008). People make up for interruptions by rushing, and they pay for it.

The cost is lopsided, too. Paul Graham's essay on the maker's schedule explains why. Managers run their day in one-hour slots, while people who make things prefer units of at least half a day. For a maker, "a single meeting can blow a whole afternoon, by breaking it into two pieces each too small to do anything hard in" (Paul Graham, Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule, 2009). Sending a quick ping costs almost nothing. Receiving it can cost the afternoon.

What happened when one team protected its time

Perlow didn't stop at the diagnosis. Together with the team, she blocked off uninterrupted time in three phases. First, three mornings a week until noon. Then interaction time from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. every day, with the hours around it left uninterrupted. Then the first setup again. The share of engineers who rated their productivity above average went from 59% in phase one to 41% in phase two and 65% in phase three. Three months after the last phase, the division's vice president credited the study with the product's on-time launch, only the second on-time launch in the division's history.

The details are more useful than the numbers:

  • Engineers had to learn to prepare. Early on they kept discovering mid-morning that they needed something from a colleague, often something they could have sorted out the day before. By phase three they had gotten better at planning ahead.
  • People started thinking about each other's focus. One engineer wrote that they used to worry only about getting more uninterrupted time for themselves, and now thought about how they affected everyone else.
  • Managers changed. They stopped running constant status checks and shifting priorities on a whim. The software manager, one of the biggest skeptics at the start, said he had learned to define a task and then give engineers time to do it.
  • Some engineers said they liked one continuous block more than a day chopped into awkward pieces.

There's a warning in the study as well. When Perlow came back months after the launch, the protected blocks had mostly faded. A later attempt to bring them back failed because, as one engineer put it, nobody had an incentive to respect them. The managers' lighter touch did last. A focus rule only sticks when the team also changes what it rewards.

Norms that give attention back

You don't need a research project to start. A few practical norms go a long way:

  • Sort requests by urgency, out loud. Agree on what counts as "interrupt me now" (production down, a customer blocked, a release stuck) and give it its own channel or tag. Everything else waits for the next natural break.
  • Put the context in the request. A review request with a filled-in description, or a question that includes the error and what you've tried, is much cheaper to pick up. Pull requests reviewers can approve without guessing has a checklist for the PR side.
  • Batch what isn't urgent. Keep a running list and ask three questions at once, instead of one every twenty minutes.
  • Write decisions down. If a meeting only exists to share information, try a short written note first and keep meetings for decisions that need back-and-forth. Keeping meeting notes close to decisions shows one way to do it.
  • Split incident roles. One person drives the fix, one handles updates, and everyone else stays on their work instead of half-watching the channel.
  • Protect a shared block. Two or three mornings a week with no meetings and no non-urgent pings, kept as one continuous stretch.

Leads set the tone

A casual question from a lead never feels casual on the receiving end. People drop what they're doing to answer, because it came from someone senior. Perlow saw the same thing with managers' status checks, and the fix there sat with the managers. If you lead a team, choose the channel and timing for your questions with the same care you'd expect in code: async by default, a note with context, and "no rush, reply after lunch" when you mean it.

Still responsive, just to the right things

Protecting focus doesn't make a team slow. Real incidents still interrupt. A blocked customer still matters. The goal is to stop paying the same immediate price for every loose thread. A team settles into a better rhythm when people trust three things: focus time is legitimate, async notes get read, and the urgent path is clearly marked.

Try it this week

  • Agree with your team on what counts as urgent and where urgent things go.
  • Pick two mornings with no meetings and no non-urgent pings, and run it for a month.
  • Before you ping someone, add the context they'd need to answer without a call.
  • If you're a lead, move your status questions to a written check-in.

faqs.q: Why are interruptions costly if people still finish their work?
faqs.a: In a CHI 2008 study by Gloria Mark and colleagues, interrupted people finished email tasks faster with the same quality, but reported more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort. They made up for the interruptions by rushing.

faqs.q: Does blocking off focus time work for a whole team?
faqs.a: It can. In Leslie Perlow's 1999 study of a software team, 59% of engineers rated their productivity above average with three uninterrupted mornings a week, and 65% when the setup was repeated. Within months the effect had mostly faded, because the team never changed what it rewarded.

faqs.q: What should count as an urgent interruption?
faqs.a: Agree on it as a team. Typical examples are production outages, a blocked customer or a stuck release. Give those their own channel or tag so everything else can wait for a natural break.

faqs.q: How can a team lead protect the team's focus?
faqs.a: Ask questions asynchronously with context, move status checks to a written check-in, and say clearly when something is not urgent. Questions from leads feel urgent to the person receiving them, even when they are casual.
